sittings.why_these_chairs: Blackstone speaks first because the report names his ratio, that it is better ten guilty escape than one innocent suffer, and because he also wrote that a free state must regulate who may vote. Madison wrote Federalist 51, which the report cites on obliging government to control itself, and Federalist 52 on the suffrage. Hamilton answers for national power: Federalist 59 defends a federal reserve over federal elections, the strongest founding case for the administration's side. Aristotle is seated because Politics III asks the prior question, who is a citizen and so who belongs in the count. Beccaria wrote on presumption of innocence and on preventing crimes rather than punishing them, the two halves of the report's precautionary dispute. The Tenth Amendment enters through Madison's Federalist 45 rather than as a separate chair. Tocqueville is left off because his writing on elections does not touch citizenship checks. The judges, the administration, state officials and the voters on the list are context only.

turn.text: Blackstone speaks of evidence; I spoke of the design that must hold whoever has the evidence. “The definition of the right of suffrage is very justly regarded as a fundamental article of republican government.” (Federalist No. 52) So the question of who may vote is not a technicality; it is the foundation. But the same paper that grants government power warns that “you must first enable the government to control the governed; and in the next place oblige it to control itself.” (Federalist No. 51) An enforcement effort against wrongful voting is government controlling the governed. A court stopping that effort from pressuring election workers is government obliged to control itself.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Aquinas speaks first because the report names just war theory and he gave it its standard form: authority, just cause and right intention. Augustine is the theory's source and its most sorrowful voice. Thucydides is named for the security dilemma, where one side's defense is the other's threat. Grotius wrote directly on whether a rival's growing power justifies striking first, and on the defensive precautions it does justify. Hobbes is the realist account of deterrence. Cicero adds the rule of last resort: force only when discussion fails. Kant is left off because his Perpetual Peace sat on this subject last night. The supreme leader, the U.S. president, the foreign minister and the Qatari mediators are context only.

Both are in copyright and appear in paraphrase only. Locke wrote the classic account of prerogative, power used for the public good outside the law, and of its limits. Burke, named for warning that radical repair can destroy what it means to save, wrote that change should preserve. Plato is seated for the guardian question the report attributes to Juvenal. Machiavelli wrote on irregular acts that restore a republic, and on the precedent they leave. Juvenal is left off because his line comes from a satire on marriage, not on courts. Madison and Hamilton, seated on this story last night, are left off to give tonight's report its own named voices. Tusk, Nawrocki, Święczkowski, Matczak and the Venice Commission are context only.

turn.text: But toleration in my sense never required anyone to think other religions true; it required that no one be harmed for his. Every church counts itself the orthodox one (A Letter Concerning Toleration, paraphrased). The bishops may teach about Islam accurately and still teach that Christianity is true. That combination is not relativism; it is the condition of peaceful disagreement.

chairs.modern_read: Locke argued that people of every religion deserve equal civil rights, so mutual understanding serves a shared civic life. Toleration does not require believing other faiths are true, so accurate teaching and firm conviction can coexist.
